You are reviewing an uncommitted implementation in a RISC-V bare-metal OS course lab at /workspace.
The relevant sources are:
  /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c
  /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c
  /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/include/os/mm.h
  /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/drivers/net.c
  /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/mm/mm.c
  /workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/sched/sched.c
Use 'git diff' in /workspace to see exactly what was added (the rest of the tree is pre-existing scaffolding).
Read supporting headers (include/os/*.h, arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h, drivers/net.h, kernel/syscall/syscall.c, init/main.c, test/*.c) to understand the intended contracts.
Both projects already COMPILE cleanly, so do not report compile errors unless you are certain.
Report only real correctness defects that would cause wrong behavior at runtime. Be concrete and cite file:line.
Focus dimension: P4 kernel/sched/sched.c — scheduler() and max_priority_node() (priority/CPU-affinity selection, per-core current_running, kernel/user stack switching, satp switch + sfence.vma on context switch, idle handling when no task is ready), do_exec (ELF load via the elf.h helpers, argc/argv setup on the user stack, allocating and mapping user pages, pid allocation), do_exit / do_kill / do_waitpid (freeing page tables, waking waiters, releasing held locks and mailboxes, not freeing the stack the CPU is currently running on).

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

#!/bin/bash
# Host-side functional tests for the kernel subsystems implemented in this repo.
#
# Kernel code is compiled natively (with small shims under hostshim/ standing in
# for the RISC-V specific headers) and driven directly, so the scheduling,
# synchronisation, IPC and file-system logic can be executed and asserted on
# without a board or an emulator.
set -u

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
ROOT=$(pwd)
SHIM="$ROOT/agent_tests/hostshim"
OUT=$(mktemp -d)
fail=0

run_case() {
    local name=$1; shift
    if ! gcc -g -O0 -o "$OUT/$name" "$@" 2>"$OUT/$name.log"; then
        echo "[$name] COMPILE FAILED"
        sed -n '1,40p' "$OUT/$name.log"
        fail=1
        return
    fi
    if ! timeout 60 "$OUT/$name"; then
        echo "[$name] RUN FAILED"
        fail=1
    fi
}

P2A="$ROOT/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1"
run_case p2a_sched \
    "$ROOT/agent_tests/p2a_sched_test.c" \
    "$P2A/kernel/sched/sched.c" "$P2A/kernel/locking/lock.c" \
    -I"$SHIM" -I"$P2A/include" -I"$P2A/drivers" -I"$P2A/arch/riscv/include"

# get_ticks() reads the RISC-V `time` CSR, which the host cannot execute.  Swap
# just that one read for a counter the test drives; timer_check() -- the code
# actually under test -- is compiled verbatim.
host_time_c() {
    python3 - "$1" "$2" <<'PY'
import sys
src = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
asm = '''    __asm__ __volatile__(
        "rdtime %0"
        : "=r"(time_elapsed));'''
assert asm in src, "get_ticks() no longer looks the way the test expects"
src = src.replace(asm, "    time_elapsed = host_get_ticks();")
src = "extern unsigned long host_get_ticks(void);\n" + src
open(sys.argv[2], "w").write(src)
PY
}

P2B="$ROOT/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2"
if [ -f "$ROOT/agent_tests/p2b_sched_test.c" ]; then

content.text: I've completed my analysis. Here are the findings.

findings.title: Interrupt-mode do_net_recv() copies the staged frames immediately after scheduler(), before the data exists and in the wrong address space
findings.detail:
In the `net_poll_mode == 1` branch `do_net_recv()` does `do_block(...); scheduler();` and then falls straight through to the copy-out loop at lines 83-93. In this kernel `scheduler()` does not switch stacks or contexts — it only rewrites `current_running[cpu_id]`, `current_cpu_running` and `satp` (kernel/sched/sched.c:70-123, entry.S `ret_from_exception` is what actually restores the next context). So every statement after `scheduler()` executes right away, on the still-current kernel stack, microseconds after the caller was queued on `net_recv_queue`.

Two things go wrong at once:
1. `XEmacPsRecvHandler()` (drivers/emacps/xemacps_main.c:914-950) has not run yet, so `recv_stage` and `recv_stage_len[]` are still all-zero. The loop copies 0 bytes per packet and `rx_tail` stays 0.
2. `scheduler()` has already executed `set_satp(..., next->pgdir)`, so the `memcpy((uint8_t*)rx_curr, ...)` at line 87 and the `*(frLength + i) = ...` at line 88 write to the *caller's* user virtual addresses while some **other** process's page table is installed — silently corrupting that process's memory, or taking a kernel-mode page fault.

`handle_syscall()` then stores the return value (0) into the blocked task's saved `a0`, so when the caller is finally woken by the handler it returns from `sys_net_recv` with length 0 and an untouched buffer. The same file's `do_waitpid()` (kernel/sched/sched.c:462-500) shows the author is aware of this constraint — it rewinds `sepc` and retries the ecall precisely because "a blocked process can only be resumed in user mode".
findings.why_wrong: `scheduler()` in this kernel is not a blocking call; the context switch happens later in `ret_from_exception`. Code placed after `scheduler()` runs synchronously with the *next* task's `satp` installed, so it can neither see the interrupt handler's results nor legally touch the caller's user memory.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not stage into kernel memory and copy afterwards. Either (a) point the handler directly at the caller's buffers before blocking — `_addr = addr; _frLength = frLength;` — which is what `_addr`/`_num_packet`/`_frLength` in drivers/net.h exist for, and return only the length after the handler ran (via the `sepc -= 4` retry trick used by `do_waitpid`), or (b) keep `recv_stage` but rewind `regs->sepc` and re-enter the syscall after wakeup so the copy-out runs in the caller's own address space. Also make sure `recv_transaction`/`rx_tail` bookkeeping is consistent on the retry path.

findings.title: release_resources() never gives back the pending `sem--` of a task killed while blocked on a binary semaphore, corrupting the semaphore's block queue
findings.detail:
`binsem_op(BINSEM_OP_LOCK)` (kernel/locking/binsem.c:36-45) does `node->sem--` and only then blocks the caller on `node->block_queue`; the id is *not* recorded in `binsem_id[]` until an unlocker hands the lock over. P5's `release_resources()` (lines 278-287) only calls `release_binsem()` (which walks `binsem_id[]`, i.e. locks actually *held*) and drains `wait_list`/the timer. `reclaim_pcb()` then does `list_del(&task->list)`, pulling the dead task off the semaphore's block queue without restoring the count.

Result: `binsem_nodes[id].sem` is left one too low with an empty `block_queue`. The next `binsem_op(BINSEM_OP_UNLOCK)` takes the `node->sem <= 0` branch (binsem.c:50-57) with an empty queue, so `list_entry(node->block_queue.next, pcb_t, list)` yields `(pcb_t*)((char*)&node->block_queue - offsetof(pcb_t, list))` — a bogus PCB. It then writes `heir->binsem_id[heir->binsem_num] = id` through that pointer (a wild store into the globals preceding `binsem_nodes[]`), and calls `do_unblock(&node->block_queue)`, which `list_del`s the queue *head* (setting its next/prev to NULL, so `list_empty()` is false forever) and splices that head into `ready_queue`. `max_priority_node()` will subsequently treat the semaphore head as a `pcb_t`.

The P4 sibling of this file has exactly the missing piece — `abandon_binsem_wait()` at Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:323-336 — and calls it from `release_resources()`; P5 dropped it.
findings.why_wrong: A task blocked on a binsem has already consumed a unit of the semaphore. Removing it from the queue without `node->sem++` leaves the counter and the queue permanently inconsistent, and the unlock path dereferences the list head as a PCB.
findings.suggested_fix: Port `abandon_binsem_wait()` from the P4 file and call it from `release_resources()` right after `release_binsem(task)`: scan every `binsem_nodes[i].block_queue` for `&task->list`, and on a match `list_del(p); node->sem++;`. (Defensively, also make `binsem_op(UNLOCK)` check `!list_empty(&node->block_queue)` before dereferencing `block_queue.next`.)

findings.title: do_waitpid() reaps AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT children that are still owned by pending_reap[]/the idle reaper, double-freeing the kernel stack and corrupting ready_queue
findings.detail:
`destroy_task()` puts an `AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT` task into `TASK_EXITED` and hands ownership to the core-0 idle reaper — either directly (line 378) or, when the task is still unwinding on its own kernel stack, one scheduling round later through `pending_reap[cpu_id]` (lines 373-376, drained at lines 78-81). `do_waitpid()` (lines 483-491), however, treats `TASK_EXITED` exactly like `TASK_ZOMBIE` and reaps it itself: `free_user_page(kva2pa(child->kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE)); list_del(&child->list); child->pid = -1;`.

Concrete two-core sequence:
1. Child C (AUTO_CLEANUP) exits on core 0. `scheduler()` -> `destroy_task(C, 1)` wakes the parent P (queued on `C->wait_list`) and sets `pending_reap[0] = C`; `C->list` is unlinked (prev/next == NULL).
2. Core 1 schedules P, which retries the waitpid ecall. `find_pcb(C)` still finds it (pid valid), `status == TASK_EXITED`, so P frees C's kernel-stack frame, `list_del(&C->list)` is a no-op, and `C->pid = -1` — the PCB slot is now free.
3. `do_exec()` (line 242) hands slot C to a new process N, which allocates a fresh kernel stack (possibly the frame just freed) and does `list_add_tail(&N->list, &ready_queue)` (line 291).
4. Core 0's next `scheduler()` runs the drain at line 79: `list_add_tail(&pending_reap[0]->list, &kernel_pcb[0].wait_list)` — but that is now `&N->list`, which is live in `ready_queue`. `_list_add` rewrites its next/prev into the wait list while `ready_queue`'s neighbours still point at it, splicing the two lists together; `max_priority_node()` then walks into `kernel_pcb[0].wait_list` and can `list_entry()` the list head as a PCB.
5. Core 0's idle loop (init/main.c:204-215) then also does `clean_pcb->pid = -1` and `free_user_page(...)` on N — killing a live process and freeing a frame that is in use.

Even without slot reuse, step 4/5 is a second `free_user_page()` on the same frame.
findings.why_wrong: Two independent reapers own the same PCB. `do_waitpid()` may only reap tasks whose teardown it owns (`ENTER_ZOMBIE_ON_EXIT` / `TASK_ZOMBIE`); an `AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT` task is owned by `pending_reap[]` and the core-0 idle loop, and `pending_reap` still holds a raw pointer to the PCB after waitpid frees the slot.
findings.suggested_fix: Only reap in the branch the caller owns: `if (child->status == TASK_ZOMBIE) { ...free stack, pid = -1... } else if (child->status == TASK_EXITED) { enable_preempt(); return 0; /* the kernel already reclaimed it */ }`. If waitpid must also work for AUTO_CLEANUP children, first take the PCB away from the other reaper (clear it from `pending_reap[]` on every core before freeing anything).

findings.title: do_kill() drains the victim's wait_list before the victim is actually reclaimed, so a do_waitpid() parent wakes up too early and blocks forever
findings.detail:
`do_kill()` calls `release_resources(victim)` unconditionally at line 362, which drains `victim->wait_list` via `do_unblock()`. When the victim is running on the *other* hart, line 369 only marks it `TASK_KILLED`; the actual reclamation happens later, in that hart's `scheduler()` (lines 98-102 -> `reclaim_pcb`), which does **not** call `release_resources()` again.

So the parent that was sleeping in `do_waitpid()` is put on `ready_queue` while `victim->status == TASK_KILLED`. Because it resumes by re-executing the ecall (`regs->sepc -= 4`, line 415), it re-enters `do_waitpid()`, finds the child neither `TASK_ZOMBIE` nor `TASK_EXITED` (line 405), and blocks again on `child->wait_list` (line 417). Nothing ever drains that list a second time — `reclaim_pcb()` only does `list_del(&task->list)` and flips the status — so the parent sleeps forever. With the big kernel lock, the killer's hart releases the lock as soon as `do_kill` returns, while the victim's hart will not reschedule until its next timer tick (up to 10 ms), so the parent almost always wins this race.
findings.why_wrong: Waiters must be woken only once the child has reached a reapable state (ZOMBIE/EXITED). Waking them while the victim is still `TASK_KILLED` makes them re-block on a queue that is never serviced again.
findings.suggested_fix: Move `release_resources(victim)` out of the early path in `do_kill()` and into the point where the task actually becomes reapable — i.e. call it from `reclaim_pcb()` (or from the `scheduler()` dying branch) just before setting `TASK_ZOMBIE`/`TASK_EXITED`, mirroring what P4's `destroy_task()` does at Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:359-381.

findings.title: reclaim_pcb() publishes the dying task to the core-0 idle reaper while it is still executing on that kernel stack
findings.detail:
`scheduler()` calls `reclaim_pcb(dying)` at line 101, and for `AUTO_CLEANUP_ON_EXIT` that immediately does `list_add_tail(&task->list, &kernel_pcb[0].wait_list)` (line 304). At that moment the dying task is still standing on its kernel stack: it has to return from `scheduler()`, out of `do_exit()`/`handle_syscall()`/`interrupt_helper()` and through `ret_from_exception` before the stack is abandoned.

Core 0's reaper loop (init/main.c:245-259) runs in the idle task's own context, i.e. *after* `unlock_kernel`, so it is not serialised by the big kernel lock. If the task died on core 1, core 0 can execute `free_user_page(kva2pa(clean_pcb->kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE))` while core 1 is still pushing/popping frames on that page; the freed frame can then be handed to `alloc_user_page()` (which `memset`s it to zero) and the unwinding core resumes on wiped stack memory. The comment above `reclaim_pcb` even asserts the stack "is released later", but nothing enforces that ordering.

The P4 sibling solves exactly this with the one-round `pending_reap[]` delay (Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:56-81, 373-376); P5 dropped it.
findings.why_wrong: Ownership of the kernel stack is transferred to a lock-free reaper on another hart before the dying task has left that stack, so the frame can be freed and reused while in use.
findings.suggested_fix: Port P4's `pending_reap[NR_CPUS]` mechanism: in the dying branch store the task in `pending_reap[cpu_id]` and only splice it into `kernel_pcb[0].wait_list` at the top of the *next* `scheduler()` call on that hart, by which time `ret_from_exception` has switched `sp` away.

findings.title: do_exec() passes the unclamped argc to init_pcb_stack(), so a0 can disagree with the argv array actually built
findings.detail:
`init_user_stack()` clamps its local copy of `argc` (lines 147-152: negative/NULL -> 0, `> MAX_EXEC_ARGC` -> 16) and only writes that many pointers plus the NULL terminator into the new user stack. But `do_exec()` calls it by value at line 246 and then hands the *original* `argc` to `init_pcb_stack()` at line 249, which stores it into `pt_regs->regs[10]` (a0) at line 122.

So if a caller passes `argc = 40`, the child's `main()` receives `argc == 40` while `argv[]` only has 16 valid entries followed by NULL — the loop in e.g. test/rw.c (`for (i = 1; i < argc; i++) atol(argv[i])`) walks off the end of the array into whatever follows on the stack page. A negative `argc` is propagated verbatim as well. There is also no page-size budget on the strings (unlike P4's version at Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c:171-184), so long arguments write below the single mapped stack page, i.e. into the adjacent physical frame via the kernel direct map.
findings.why_wrong: The `argc` handed to the process must describe the array that was actually built; clamping one and not the other lets the child read past the end of argv.
findings.suggested_fix: Take `int *argc_io` in `init_user_stack()` and write the clamped value back (as the P4 version does), then pass `*argc_io` to `init_pcb_stack()`. Additionally add P4's size budget so the strings + argv array are guaranteed to fit in the one mapped stack page.

findings.title: write_to_sd() only flushes the local TLB, leaving the other hart with a stale writable mapping of a swapped-out frame
findings.detail:
`write_to_sd()` clears `_PAGE_PRESENT`, sets `_PAGE_SOFT`, repoints the PFN at the swap slot and then calls `local_flush_tlb_all()` (line 161) before `free_user_page(pa)`. The evicted frame can belong to a process that is currently running on the *other* hart (`selete_page()` picks any unpinned frame, mm.c:104-116, and NR_CPUS is 2). That hart keeps its cached writable translation, so it goes on writing into a frame that has already been marked free and can be handed to `alloc_user_page()` for a different address space (which also `memset`s it).

The same downgrade from `flush_tlb_all()` to `local_flush_tlb_all()` was applied to `free_process_user_page()` (line 269), `alloc_page_helper()` (line 346) and the shm paths (lines 373, 400). The P4 version of this file uses `flush_tlb_all()` (which adds `sbi_remote_sfence_vma`) in all of these places.
findings.why_wrong: Revoking or re-pointing a PTE that may be live in another hart's TLB requires a remote shootdown; `sfence.vma` only affects the issuing hart.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `flush_tlb_all()` (local sfence + `sbi_remote_sfence_vma`) wherever a mapping is removed or repointed — at minimum in `write_to_sd()` and `free_process_user_page()`. `local_flush_tlb_all()` is only safe for pure additions to the page table of the hart-local address space.

content.content: Structured output provided successfully
